etymology: From Old North French werre, from a Germanic root meaning confusion or strife — the Romance languages took the word from the Franks because Latin's own bellum died out in the vernacular. The Hebrew milchāmâh comes from lācham, to fight, a verb that also means to eat or devour, so that in Hebrew war is named as a consuming. The English keeps the note of confusion; the Hebrew keeps the note of appetite.
biblical_def: Scripture neither romanticises war nor pretends it can be abolished before Christ returns. The Preacher lists it among the appointed seasons of a fallen world — “a time of war, and a time of peace” (Ecc 3:8) — and James traces its origin inward: from whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? War is therefore a symptom of the fall, not an accident of policy. Yet the LORD Himself takes the title: “The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name” (Exo 15:3), sung at the Red Sea when He had fought for a people who held their peace. He is not embarrassed by the name, and He teaches His servants to use the sword when He appoints it — “Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight” (Psa 144:1). At the same time the decisive warfare of the church is of another kind altogether: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4), and the strong holds named are imaginations and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God. The Christian therefore holds two things at once: the magistrate bears the sword, and beareth it not in vain, as God's minister for the punishment of evildoers; and the church advances by the word, by prayer, and by suffering, never by the sword. The end of war is promised but not by human achievement — they shall beat their swords into plowshares when the LORD judges among the nations.
webster_summary: Open armed conflict between nations or parties; in Scripture a consequence of the fall traced by James to inward lust, a season appointed under providence, a title the LORD takes as the deliverer of His people, and something wholly distinct from the church's warfare, whose weapons are not carnal.
webster_full: WAR, n. 1. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs.
2. In Scripture, the LORD is called a man of war, as the deliverer of his people and the avenger of their enemies. Exod. 15.
3. Enmity; state of opposition. The carnal mind is enmity against God; and the flesh lusteth against the spirit.
4. Spiritual warfare; the Christian's conflict with the world, the flesh, and the devil, carried on with weapons that are not carnal. 2 Cor. 10; Eph. 6.
5. To make war; to invade. To be at war; to be in a state of hostility. Man of war; a ship of the line, and in Scripture a warrior.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 3:8
A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace.
Exodus 15:3
The LORD is a man of war: the LORD is his name.
2 Corinthians 10:4
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Psalm 144:1
A Psalm of David. Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight:
corruption_summary: Two errors divide the ground: a pacifism that reads the Sermon on the Mount as abolishing the magistrate's sword, and a militarism that baptises a nation's wars as the LORD's — both collapsing the distinction Scripture keeps between the church and the civil sphere.
corruption_paragraphs: The pacifist reading takes resist not evil and turn the other cheek as a rule for magistrates as well as for private men. But the same apostolic writing that forbids the Christian to avenge himself — dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves — immediately grounds the prohibition in the fact that God has appointed someone else to do it: the magistrate is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil, and beareth not the sword in vain. Private vengeance is forbidden precisely because public justice is ordained. John the Baptist did not tell the soldiers to leave their calling but to do violence to no man and be content with their wages, and Cornelius the centurion is commended without any hint that his office was sin.

The opposite error is far more flattering to a nation and therefore more dangerous to a church. Where a country's wars are treated as holy wars, the conquest narratives of Joshua are misapplied to modern states, and the language of Zion is transferred to a flag. Israel's wars of conquest were a unique, commanded, and bounded judgment on the iniquity of the Amorites, executed by a nation under a theocratic covenant that has no successor state. No modern nation stands where Israel stood. The classical Christian answer — that a war may be just when it is declared by lawful authority, for a just cause, with right intention, as a last resort, and waged with restraint toward the innocent — is a discipline of restraint, not a license, and it remains the wiser path between the two errors.
roots_summary: Hebrew milchāmâh, from lācham (to fight, also to devour), names war as a consuming; tsābā' is the host or army, whence LORD of hosts. Greek polemos is war and strateia the campaign or warfare, the word of 2Co 10:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew milchāmâh (H4421) — war, battle; some 319 occurrences, from the wars of the LORD to the day of battle.
Hebrew lācham (H3898) — to fight, to do battle; the same consonants also bear the sense to eat, and lechem is bread — war as a devouring.
Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — an army, a host, warfare; the word in the divine title the LORD of hosts, some 285 occurrences.
Greek polemos (G4171) — war, battle; used of wars and rumours of wars (Mat 24:6) and of the war in heaven (Rev 12:7).
Greek strateia (G4752) — a military campaign, warfare; used in 2Co 10:4 of the weapons of our warfare and in 1Ti 1:18 of warring a good warfare.
usage: Of appointed seasons and their origin: a time of war, and a time of peace (Ecc 3:8); from whence come wars and fightings among you? (Jas 4:1).
Of the LORD as warrior for His people: the LORD is a man of war (Exo 15:3); the LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace (Exo 14:14).
Of the church's different warfare: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal (2Co 10:4); we wrestle not against flesh and blood (Eph 6:12).

etymology: From Old French bataille, from Late Latin battualia, fencing exercises, from battuere, to beat. A battle is properly the single engagement, as distinguished from the war of which it is a part — and the Authorized Version keeps that distinction reasonably well, using battle for the day of engagement and the array of troops (as in the horse is prepared against the day of battle).
biblical_def: Scripture's doctrine of battle is stated in one sentence by a boy with a sling: “the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands” (1Sa 17:47), and David says it after declaring that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. The lesson is repeated to a whole kingdom by Jahaziel in Jehoshaphat's crisis: “Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15) — and Judah went out with singers before the army. The doctrine does not abolish preparation; it puts preparation in its place. Solomon states the balance exactly: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). The horse is to be prepared — the proverb assumes it — and the outcome still belongs to God, which is neither fatalism nor self-reliance but the ordinary Reformed account of means under providence. The title that gathers it all is in the psalm of the ascending King: “Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle” (Psa 24:8). The New Testament transposes the whole vocabulary without softening it: the Christian's day of battle is the evil day, his array is the whole armour of God, and his victory is already secured by a Lord who spoiled principalities and powers and triumphed over them openly.
webster_summary: A single armed engagement; in Scripture the appointed occasion on which it is shewn that safety is of the LORD — the horse prepared and the outcome God's — and the source of the divine title, the LORD mighty in battle.
webster_full: BATTLE, n. 1. A fight, or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
2. A body of forces, or division of an army, drawn up in array. The battle of the Israelites was set in array against the Philistines.
3. In Scripture, the day of battle is the day of trial and of deliverance, in which it is made manifest that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. 1 Sam. 17.
4. To join battle; to meet in hostile encounter. To give battle; to attack an enemy.
5. The LORD mighty in battle; a title of Jehovah as the deliverer and King of glory. Psalm 24.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:47
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
2 Chronicles 20:15

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
Proverbs 21:31
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
Psalm 24:8
Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle.
corruption_summary: “The battle is the LORD's” is used to excuse the neglect of ordinary means, as though preparation were unbelief; and in the other direction the language of spiritual battle is used to dramatise personal difficulties until every inconvenience becomes warfare.
corruption_paragraphs: The passivity error takes 2Ch 20:15 as a rule against effort. But even in that chapter Judah was told to go down against them and to set themselves and stand still; they marched, they arrayed, and they went in order. David ran toward the Philistine, and he had chosen five smooth stones out of the brook. Pro 21:31 is the settled statement of the principle: the horse is prepared, and safety is of the LORD. Reformed theology has always insisted that God ordains the means along with the end, so that trusting providence is a reason for diligence rather than a substitute for it. The man who will not prepare the horse is not trusting God; he is tempting Him.

The opposite inflation is now common in devotional speech, where every setback is called a battle, every critic an enemy, and every difficulty spiritual warfare, until the vocabulary is worn out and cannot be used when a real conflict comes. Scripture is more sober. It names the actual enemies — principalities, powers, the rulers of the darkness of this world, spiritual wickedness in high places — and it names the actual weapons, which are truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer. Nothing in that list is a technique for winning arguments or removing inconveniences, and a Christian who has learned to call his irritations warfare will be poorly equipped when the evil day actually arrives.
roots_summary: Hebrew uses the same word for war and battle, milchāmâh, with ma'ārākâh for the battle array or line drawn up. Greek polemos is the conflict; parataxis, the drawing up in order, lies behind the military imagery of the epistles.
roots_lines: Hebrew milchāmâh (H4421) — war, battle, the engagement itself; the word of the battle is the LORD'S in 1Sa 17:47.
Hebrew ma'ārākâh (H4634) — a rank or row, an army set in array; used repeatedly in the Goliath narrative of the armies drawn up against each other.
Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — host, army, service; the divine title LORD of hosts is a battle title before it is anything else.
Greek polemos (G4171) — war, battle; used of the battle of that great day of God Almighty (Rev 16:14).
Greek panoplia (G3833) — the full armour of a heavy infantryman; the word of Eph 6:11, the whole armour of God, presupposing a day of battle.
usage: Of the LORD's ownership of the outcome: the battle is the LORD'S (1Sa 17:47); the battle is not yours, but God's (2Ch 20:15).
Of means and providence together: the horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD (Pro 21:31).
Of the divine warrior and the last conflict: the LORD mighty in battle (Psa 24:8); gather them to the battle of that great day (Rev 16:14).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew shālāl, baz, and Greek skula, apekduomai)
etymology: From Old French espoillier, from Latin spoliare, to strip — from spolium, the hide stripped from an animal and thence the armour stripped from a defeated enemy. The original sense is stripping, and both the Hebrew shālāl and the Greek skula keep it: spoil is what is taken off the vanquished. The modern English sense of to ruin is a later development from the same stripping figure.
biblical_def: Spoil is what victory takes, and Scripture uses it in three ascending senses. Historically, it is plunder: at the Exodus “they spoiled the Egyptians” (Exo 12:36), the LORD having given the people favour so that the goods of their oppressors went out with them — back wages for four centuries of unpaid labour, and the material out of which the tabernacle would later be built. Prophetically, it belongs to the Servant: “he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death” (Isa 53:12), the only conqueror in Scripture who wins the spoil by dying. Doctrinally, Paul brings it to its head at the cross: “having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:15) — the imagery is a Roman triumph in which the defeated are stripped of their arms and led publicly behind the victor's chariot, and the powers so treated are the spiritual ones that held men under the handwriting of ordinances. The place where the cross looked most like defeat is named by the apostle as the place of the stripping and the parade. Finally, the psalmist takes the figure and applies it to Scripture itself: “I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil” (Psa 119:162) — the joy of the soldier who opens a captured tent, applied to a man opening his Bible.
webster_summary: That which is taken by force from an enemy; in Scripture the goods of Egypt given to Israel at the Exodus, the portion the dying Servant divides with the strong, the arms stripped from principalities and powers at the cross, and the psalmist's figure for the joy of finding God's word.
webster_full: SPOIL, v.t. 1. To plunder; to strip by violence; to rob. They spoiled the Egyptians. Exod. 12.
2. To seize by violence; to take by force. Lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit. Col. 2.
3. To corrupt; to cause to decay and perish; whence the modern common use of the word.
4. SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; pillage; plunder; particularly the arms and armor stripped from a vanquished enemy.
5. To divide the spoil; to share the fruits of a victory. He shall divide the spoil with the strong. Isa. 53.
scriptures: Exodus 12:36
And the LORD gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent unto them such things as they required. And they spoiled the Egyptians.
Isaiah 53:12

Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
Luke 11:22
But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils.
Psalm 119:162
I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil.
corruption_summary: The spoiling of the Egyptians is charged as divinely sanctioned theft, and Col 2:15 is quietly reduced to a metaphor for encouragement — when the first was restitution and the second is the objective defeat of real powers.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection to Exo 12:36 is old and is usually pressed as a moral scandal: God, it is said, commanded His people to borrow with no intention of returning. The text does not say that. The Hebrew verb rendered lent means simply to ask or request, and the Egyptians gave what was asked because the LORD gave the people favour in their sight. More to the point, Israel had built store cities for four hundred years without wages, and the law God would shortly give commands that a freed servant not be sent away empty but furnished liberally out of the flock and the floor. What happened at the Exodus is the pattern of that very law applied to a nation. The goods were not stolen; they were the severance owed to emancipated slaves, and much of it was afterward given back to God for the making of the tabernacle.

Col 2:15 suffers a gentler loss. It is often read as a general assurance that Christians should feel confident, with the principalities and powers treated as figures of speech for difficulty or fear. Paul means something objective and public. There were real rulers and authorities holding real claims over men through the law's just condemnation; the handwriting of ordinances that was against us was nailed to the cross, and with the claim cancelled the claimants were disarmed. That is why the passage begins with a legal document and ends with a triumph. The pastoral force follows from the fact, not from a mood: because the powers have actually been stripped, the Colossians need not submit to ordinances, philosophy, angel worship, or the judgment of anyone in respect of meat, drink, or holy days.
roots_summary: Hebrew shālāl is booty or plunder; baz is spoil taken in a raid. Greek skula is arms stripped from the slain, and apekduomai, the verb in Col 2:15, means to strip off completely — the same verb used of putting off the old man.
roots_lines: Hebrew shālāl (H7998) — spoil, plunder, booty; the word in Isa 53:12 and in the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, haste to the spoil (Isa 8:1).
Hebrew baz (H957) — spoil, prey; used of Judah given for a spoil and of the nations that spoiled Israel.
Greek skula (G4661) — arms and armour stripped from a defeated foe; used in Luk 11:22, where the stronger man taketh from him all his armour and divideth his spoils.
Greek apekduomai (G554) — to strip off wholly, to disarm; the verb of Col 2:15, and used again in Col 3:9 of putting off the old man with his deeds.
Greek thriambeuō (G2358) — to lead in triumph; the verb behind triumphing over them, drawn from the Roman triumphal procession.
usage: Of plunder in history: they spoiled the Egyptians (Exo 12:36); the spoil of the Midianites divided (Num 31:27).
Of the Servant's reward: he shall divide the spoil with the strong (Isa 53:12).
Of the cross and of the word: having spoiled principalities and powers (Col 2:15); I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil (Psa 119:162).

etymology: From Late Latin capitaneus, chief, from caput, the head — a captain is literally a head man. That etymology matters for the New Testament's most striking use, since the Greek archēgos is built the same way: archē, beginning or rule, plus agō, to lead — one who goes first and thereby opens the way for those who follow. The Authorized Version renders it captain in Heb 2:10 and author in Heb 12:2, and both senses are in the word.
biblical_def: The captain in Scripture is the head man who leads from the front, and the term runs from ordinary military rank up to a title of Christ. At the plain level it is Naaman, “captain of the host of the king of Syria…a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2Ki 5:1) — the rank stated with the disease in the same breath, which is the whole point of his story. It can be the office men appoint in unbelief: “Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt” (Num 14:4), the congregation proposing a leader to march them back into the house of bondage. It can also be an appearance of the LORD Himself. Outside Jericho a man stood with his sword drawn, and to Joshua's challenge answered, “Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come” (Jos 5:14) — and Joshua fell on his face and worshipped, and was told to loose his shoe, for the place was holy. The One who declines to be either for Joshua or for his adversaries, and who receives worship, is no created angel. The title reaches its height in Hebrews: God brought many sons unto glory by making “the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” (Heb 2:10). Perfect here is not moral improvement — He was without sin — but the completing of Him for His office as the file-leader who has gone through death ahead of His people and opened the way.
webster_summary: A head man or commander; in Scripture an ordinary military rank, an office men propose in unbelief, a self-designation of the LORD before Jericho, and above all the title of Christ as the captain of our salvation, made perfect through sufferings to bring many sons to glory.
webster_full: CAPTAIN, n. 1. A head or chief officer; the military officer who commands a company, whether of infantry or cavalry.
2. A chief commander; a leader of a host. Captain of the host; the commander in chief of an army. 2 Kings 5.
3. The word is from the Latin caput, the head; and answers to the Hebrew sar, a prince or chief, and rosh, a head.
4. In Scripture, a title of Christ, the captain of our salvation, who is the leader and forerunner of his people. Heb. 2.
5. Captain of the host of the LORD; he that appeared to Joshua by Jericho with his sword drawn, and received worship. Josh. 5.
scriptures: Hebrews 2:10
For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
Joshua 5:14
And he said, Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come. And Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship, and said unto him, What saith my lord unto his servant?
2 Kings 5:1

Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.
Numbers 14:4
And they said one to another, Let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt.
corruption_summary: Heb 2:10 is read as though Christ needed moral improvement before He could save, and the appearance to Joshua is flattened into an ordinary angel — both readings surrendering something Scripture is careful to guard.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings has been used to argue that Jesus grew out of imperfection into holiness, and thus that His sinlessness was an achievement rather than a constant. The Greek teleioō means to bring to completion or to the appointed end, and it is used elsewhere of consecrating a priest to his office. The writer to the Hebrews states Christ's sinlessness in the plainest terms — in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin — so whatever the perfecting is, it is not the removal of fault. It is the completing of the Son in His office as captain: He has actually suffered, actually died, and actually passed through, and therefore is able to succour them that are tempted and to lead them the way He has already gone.

The other reduction concerns Jos 5. The captain of the host of the LORD is often treated as simply an angel, but the passage resists it at two points. He accepts Joshua's worship, which created angels expressly refuse — see thou do it not, worship God — and He tells Joshua to loose his shoe from off his foot, the identical command given to Moses out of the burning bush by the One who said, I AM THAT I AM. The Reformed reading has long taken this as a christophany, an appearance of the eternal Son before the incarnation. His answer to Joshua's question is also worth keeping: asked whether He was for Israel or for their adversaries, He answered Nay — He had not come to take a side but to take command.
roots_summary: Hebrew sar is a chief or prince, rosh a head; both are rendered captain. Greek archēgos is the file-leader, founder, or originator, and chiliarchos the commander of a thousand, the rank of the Roman officer in Acts.
roots_lines: Hebrew sar (H8269) — a chief, ruler, prince, captain; some 421 occurrences, from the captain of the guard to the Prince of princes.
Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, chief, top; rendered captain where headship over a body of men is meant, as in Num 14:4.
Greek archēgos (G747) — a leader who goes first, an originator, a prince; rendered captain (Heb 2:10), author (Heb 12:2), and Prince (Act 3:15; 5:31).
Greek chiliarchos (G5506) — a commander of a thousand, a tribune; the officer who rescued Paul from the mob in Jerusalem (Act 21:31).
Greek teleioō (G5048) — to complete, to bring to the appointed end, to consecrate to office; the verb rendered make perfect in Heb 2:10.
usage: Of ordinary rank: Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria (2Ki 5:1); the captain of the guard (Gen 37:36).
Of an office proposed in unbelief: let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt (Num 14:4).
Of Christ and of the LORD's host: the captain of their salvation (Heb 2:10); captain of the host of the LORD am I now come (Jos 5:14).

etymology: From Old French prince, from Latin princeps — literally first-taker, from primus (first) and capere (to take), the one who takes first place. The Hebrew words behind it are various: sar, a chief; nāgīd, a leader or one set in front; and nāsī', one lifted up, from a root meaning to raise. All three name rule as elevation, which is exactly the note Scripture turns on its head in Christ.
biblical_def: Prince in Scripture covers three ranks of being. Among men it is the chief under a king — the princes of Judah, the princes of the provinces — and Isaiah promises a ruler of another order altogether: “his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace” (Isa 9:6). The titles ascend to deity and end at peace, which is what His government secures; and of the increase of His government and peace there shall be no end. Peter preaches Him under the same word: “Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins” (Act 5:31) — and it is worth noting that repentance is there something He gives, not merely something He demands. Among angels the term names created rulers with charge over nations: the angel who came to Daniel was withstood by “the prince of the kingdom of Persia…but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan 10:13), a window into conflict in the unseen realm behind the affairs of empires. And of Satan the New Testament uses the title with deliberate irony — “the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience” (Eph 2:2), and elsewhere the prince of this world, who is judged, and shall be cast out. His princedom is real, bounded, usurped, and already sentenced.
webster_summary: A chief or ruler taking first place; in Scripture a human noble under a king, an angelic ruler set over nations, the usurped title of Satan as prince of the power of the air, and the royal titles of Christ — Prince of Peace, and a Prince and a Saviour exalted to give repentance and forgiveness.
webster_full: PRINCE, n. 1. In a general sense, a sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation or state.
2. A son of a king or emperor, or the issue of a royal family; as princes of the blood.
3. A chief in rank or in any body of men. The princes of the Philistines; the princes of Judah.
4. The chief of any body of beings. Prince of Peace, a title of the Messiah. Isa. 9. Prince of the power of the air, a title of Satan. Eph. 2.
5. The word is from the Latin princeps, first, chief; and in Scripture answers to several Hebrew terms signifying a chief, a leader, or one lifted up.
scriptures: Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
Acts 5:31
Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins.
Ephesians 2:2
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Daniel 10:13
But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
corruption_summary: Isa 9:6 is emptied by the claim that everlasting Father confuses the Persons or that the titles are mere court flattery, and Satan's princedom is inflated by a popular demonology that treats him as God's near-equal rather than as a sentenced usurper.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes are made with Isa 9:6. Some deny that the verse speaks of deity at all, treating The mighty God as the ordinary hyperbole of an ancient enthronement oracle. But the same prophet uses that exact phrase of Jehovah a chapter later — the remnant shall return unto the mighty God — and no Israelite king was ever named so. Others, granting the deity, stumble at The everlasting Father as though it confused the Son with the Father. It does not. The Hebrew idiom father of denotes the author or possessor of a thing, so that the title means the Father of eternity, the One to whom the ages belong — a claim of eternal existence, not a merging of Persons. The Trinity is not threatened by the verse; it is required by it.

The other corruption is in the reading of Satan's title. A popular demonology, encouraged by fiction and by a certain style of deliverance ministry, treats the prince of the power of the air as a rival power engaged with God in a contest of uncertain outcome. Scripture never grants this. He is a creature; he asked permission to sift Peter and to touch Job; the Lord says the prince of this world is judged and shall be cast out; and Col 2:15 has already shewn him stripped and paraded. His power over the children of disobedience is real, and Eph 2 is describing what every believer was rescued from — but the same chapter goes straight on to say that God, who is rich in mercy, quickened us together with Christ and seated us in heavenly places. The dominion is broken, and the dwelling is changed.
roots_summary: Hebrew sar (a chief), nāgīd (one set in front), and nāsī' (one lifted up) are all rendered prince. Greek archōn is a ruler, and archēgos the originator or file-leader, rendered Prince in Act 5:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew sar (H8269) — chief, prince, captain; used of human nobles and of the angelic princes of Dan 10.
Hebrew nāgīd (H5057) — a leader, one placed in front; the word in Dan 9:25, Messiah the Prince, and of David as ruler over Israel.
Hebrew nāsī' (H5387) — one lifted up, a chief; from nāsā', to raise. Used of the tribal princes of Numbers and of the prince in Ezekiel's temple vision.
Greek archōn (G758) — a ruler, chief, magistrate; used of the prince of this world (Joh 12:31) and of the rulers of the Jews.
Greek archēgos (G747) — author, originator, prince; rendered Prince in Act 3:15 (the Prince of life) and Act 5:31, and captain in Heb 2:10.
usage: Of human rulers: the princes of the Philistines (1Sa 29:4); the princes of Judah (Psa 68:27).
Of angelic and demonic rulers: the prince of the kingdom of Persia (Dan 10:13); the prince of the power of the air (Eph 2:2); the prince of this world (Joh 12:31).
Of Christ: the Prince of Peace (Isa 9:6); a Prince and a Saviour (Act 5:31); the Prince of life (Act 3:15); Messiah the Prince (Dan 9:25).

etymology: From Old English cwēn, which meant simply woman or wife — cognate with Greek gunē, woman, and with Gothic qēns. The word rose in dignity over centuries from woman to king's wife to reigning sovereign. Hebrew keeps distinctions English lost: malkâh is a reigning queen or a foreign queen, shēgal is the royal consort, and g'bīrâh is the queen mother — an office of real standing in Judah, since the mother of the reigning king is named in the formula for nearly every reign.
biblical_def: Scripture's queens fall into sharply distinguished classes. There is the queen raised up for the deliverance of God's people: Ahasuerus “set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti” (Est 2:17), and Mordecai's question — who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? — states the doctrine of providence that governs the whole book, in which God is never named and never absent. There is the queen who comes seeking wisdom: “when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions” (1Ki 10:1) — and the Lord Jesus made her a witness against His own generation, for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and a greater than Solomon is here. There is the honoured consort of the royal wedding psalm: “upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Psa 45:9), a psalm the New Testament applies to Christ and which the church has long read of Him and His bride. And there is the counterfeit: the “queen of heaven” to whom the women of Judah burned incense and poured out drink offerings (Jer 44:17), defending the practice to Jeremiah's face on the ground that it had once brought them plenty. Scripture also gives Jezebel and Athaliah, queens who ruled and destroyed, so that the office is honoured or condemned by the character and worship of the woman who holds it.
webster_summary: The wife of a king, or a woman who reigns; in Scripture Esther raised up for a providential deliverance, the queen of Sheba who came seeking wisdom and became a witness against unbelief, the honoured consort of the royal psalm, and the false queen of heaven whose worship Jeremiah rebuked.
webster_full: QUEEN, n. 1. The consort of a king; a queen consort.
2. A woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom; a queen regent; as Elizabeth, queen of England; the queen of Sheba.
3. The word is the Saxon cwen, a woman or wife, answering to the Greek gune; it has risen in dignity from its original sense.
4. Queen mother; the mother of the reigning prince, an office of dignity in the kingdom of Judah, whose name is recorded with each king's reign.
5. Queen of heaven; the title of the idol worshipped by the apostate women of Judah, to whom they burnt incense and poured out drink offerings. Jer. 7; Jer. 44.
scriptures: Esther 2:17

And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti.
1 Kings 10:1
And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.
Psalm 45:9
Kings' daughters were among thy honourable women: upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir.
Jeremiah 44:17

But we will certainly do whatsoever thing goeth forth out of our own mouth, to burn incense unto the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto her, as we have done, we, and our fathers, our kings, and our princes, in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem: for then had we plenty of victuals, and were well, and saw no evil.
corruption_summary: The title queen of heaven, which Jeremiah records as the name of an idol under judgment, was later applied to the mother of our Lord — a devotion Scripture never authorises and which Jer 44 expressly rebukes.
corruption_paragraphs: Jer 44 is one of the most direct confrontations in the prophets, and its subject is precisely this title. The women of Judah in Egypt told Jeremiah they would go on burning incense to the queen of heaven, and their argument is worth noting because it is still used: things went better for us when we did it. The prophet's answer is that the LORD remembered that incense, and that it was the cause of the desolation they were living in. The later application of the same title to the Virgin Mary, together with the doctrines of her immaculate conception, bodily assumption, and mediation, has no warrant in Scripture. Mary is blessed among women, as she herself says all generations shall call her — and her own recorded words point away from herself: whatsoever he saith unto you, do it. To honour her as the faithful mother of our Lord is right; to invoke her, crown her, or make her a mediatrix is to give to a creature what belongs to God alone, for there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

A second and quite different corruption attaches to Esther, whose book is sometimes dismissed as secular because God is not named in it, or else moralised into a story about a brave young woman being true to herself. Both readings miss the machinery. The book is an extended demonstration of providence working through ordinary means and remarkable coincidences — a sleepless king, a chronicle read at midnight, a gallows built fifty cubits high by the man who would hang on it. Esther's courage is real and is presented as costly, and it rests on Mordecai's assurance that deliverance would arise from another place if she failed. That is not self-actualisation; it is the confidence that God's purpose does not depend on the obedience He nevertheless requires.
roots_summary: Hebrew distinguishes malkâh, a reigning or foreign queen; shēgal, the royal consort; and g'bīrâh, the queen mother, a formal office in Judah. Greek basilissa is the feminine of basileus, king.
roots_lines: Hebrew malkâh (H4436) — queen; the word used of Esther, of Vashti, and of the queen of Sheba, feminine of melek, king.
Hebrew g'bīrâh (H1377) — a mistress, a queen mother; from gābar, to be strong. Asa removed Maachah from being g'bīrâh because she had made an idol (1Ki 15:13).
Hebrew shēgal (H7694) — a royal consort; the word rendered queen in Psa 45:9, standing at the king's right hand in gold of Ophir.
Hebrew m'leketh hashshāmayim — queen of heaven; the title of the Assyro-Babylonian goddess Ishtar, worshipped by apostate Judah (Jer 7:18; 44:17).
Greek basilissa (G938) — queen; used of the queen of the south (Mat 12:42), of Candace queen of the Ethiopians (Act 8:27), and of Babylon's boast, I sit a queen (Rev 18:7).
usage: Of providential elevation: made her queen instead of Vashti (Est 2:17); for such a time as this (Est 4:14).
Of the seeker after wisdom: the queen of Sheba came to prove him with hard questions (1Ki 10:1); the queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment (Mat 12:42).
Of false worship and of judgment: the queen of heaven (Jer 44:17); I sit a queen, and am no widow (Rev 18:7).

etymology: From Old English hāþen, one dwelling on the heath — the open uncultivated country, away from town and church. The formation mirrors Latin paganus, a country-dweller, which became the word for a pagan by the same route: the old religion lingered longest in the villages after the towns were christianised. In the Authorized Version the word carries no note of contempt for a race; it translates the ordinary Hebrew and Greek words for the nations, that is, the peoples outside the covenant.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version heathen, nations, and Gentiles all render one Hebrew word and one Greek word, and the category is covenantal rather than ethnic: the heathen are the peoples who do not know the LORD. Scripture's treatment of them has a settled shape. They rage against His anointed and are told it is vain — “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” (Psa 2:1) — and in the same psalm they are given to the Son as an estate: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). That is the missionary charter of the Old Testament, and it is a promise of possession by a King, not a hope of gradual improvement. God's stated end is His own exaltation among them: “Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth” (Psa 46:10) — a verse commonly quoted as a call to inward calm, though its actual subject is the LORD's public triumph over raging nations. Their religion is described without flattery: their idols are silver and gold, and in prayer “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). Yet the whole movement of Scripture is toward their ingathering — in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed — and the Great Commission sends the church to disciple all nations, the same word.
webster_summary: The nations outside the covenant; a category defined by ignorance of the true God rather than by race, described in Scripture as raging vainly against His anointed, given to the Son as His inheritance, and appointed to be discipled by the church.
webster_full: HEATHEN, n. 1. A pagan; a Gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
2. In Scripture, the word answers to the Hebrew goyim and the Greek ethne, and is rendered indifferently heathen, nations, or Gentiles.
3. The word is from heath, the open country; as pagan is from pagus, a village; both from the fact that the old idolatry lingered longest in the country places.
4. A rude, illiterate, barbarous person; a secondary and modern use, not the sense of the sacred writers.
5. HEATHEN, a. Gentile; pagan; as heathen worship; heathen nations. Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance. Psalm 2.
scriptures: Psalm 2:1
Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?
Psalm 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Matthew 6:7
But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.
Psalm 46:10
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
corruption_summary: The word is now heard as a racial slur and the biblical category discarded with it, so that the actual distinction Scripture draws — between those who know God and those who do not — is lost, along with the missionary obligation that follows from it.
corruption_paragraphs: In the Authorized Version heathen is a covenantal term with no racial content whatever: Israel herself is called a nation, and the same word describes her when she behaves like the peoples around her. The corruption came later, when European powers used the word to mark colonised peoples as inferior, and the term acquired the contempt that now clings to it. The right response is not to abolish the distinction but to recover its actual basis. Scripture teaches one blood — God hath made of one blood all nations of men — and one problem, since all have sinned, and one remedy offered to all without distinction. A category that unites every people in the same need and offers every people the same Saviour is the opposite of a racial hierarchy, and it was Christian missions working from precisely this text that produced the first sustained arguments against slavery and against the doctrine of separate human origins.

The second and now more common error, inside the churches, is to hold that the heathen are safe in their ignorance, so that the mission is at best a kindness and at worst an intrusion. Rom 1 forecloses it: what may be known of God is manifest in them, the invisible things being clearly seen by the things that are made, so that they are without excuse. And Rom 10 states the necessity plainly by a chain of questions — how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? The urgency of missions rests on that argument. Psa 2 gives the encouragement that goes with it: the nations rage, and the Father has already given them to the Son.
roots_summary: Hebrew gōy (plural gōyīm) is a nation or people, used both of Israel and of the peoples around her. Greek ethnos is its equivalent, and the Authorized Version renders both as heathen, nations, or Gentiles according to context.
roots_lines: Hebrew gōy (H1471) — a nation, a people; some 560 occurrences. Used of Israel as a great nation (Gen 12:2) as well as of the peoples outside the covenant.
Hebrew 'am (H5971) — a people, kindred; more often used of Israel as the LORD's own people, standing in contrast to gōyīm.
Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a people, the Gentiles; the word in the Great Commission, teach all nations (Mat 28:19).
Greek Hellēn (G1672) — a Greek, and by extension any Gentile; used in the pairing Jew and Greek to divide the whole human race.
Greek battologeō (G945) — to babble, to repeat vainly; the verb in Mat 6:7 describing the heathen manner of prayer.
usage: Of vain opposition and of promised possession: why do the heathen rage (Psa 2:1); I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance (Psa 2:8).
Of false religion: their idols are silver and gold (Psa 115:4); use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do (Mat 6:7).
Of God's purpose among them: I will be exalted among the heathen (Psa 46:10); declare his glory among the heathen (1Ch 16:24); teach all nations (Mat 28:19).

etymology: From Latin inhabitare, to dwell in — in plus habitare, to have habitually, to dwell. The Hebrew is the active participle of yāshab, to sit or dwell, so that an inhabitant is literally one sitting in a place: the same verb behind sit. Dwelling in Scripture's idiom is a settled sitting rather than a mere location, and the inhabitants of a land are those who have taken their seat in it.
biblical_def: Scripture speaks of inhabitants in order to say two things about them: they are small before God, and they are accountable to Him. The smallness is Isaiah's: “It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain” (Isa 40:22). The comparison is not contempt but proportion, and the chapter uses it to comfort a people who thought their way was hid from the LORD. The accountability is everywhere: “The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant” (Isa 24:5) — a remarkable verse, since it charges the whole earth's population with breach of a covenant, which points back past Sinai to the creation ordinance and the covenant with Noah binding on all mankind. The proper response of inhabitants to their Maker is therefore reverence: “Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him” (Psa 33:8). And the term carries an eschatological weight in Revelation, where the dwellers on earth are those whose settled home and hope are here: “Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time” (Rev 12:12). Against them stand the saints, who are strangers and pilgrims, inhabitants of no city they can see.
webster_summary: One who dwells or resides permanently in a place; in Scripture the earth's population viewed under God — as grasshoppers before His greatness, as accountable for a defiled earth and a broken everlasting covenant, and as summoned to stand in awe of Him.
webster_full: INHABITANT, n. 1. One who dwells or resides permanently in a place, or who has a fixed residence, as distinguished from an occasional lodger or visitor.
2. In Scripture, the word renders a Hebrew participle signifying one sitting or settled in a place; hence dwelling denotes a settled abode, and not mere presence.
3. The inhabitants of the earth; mankind considered as dwelling upon it under the government of God. Psalm 33; Isa. 24.
4. The inhabiters of the earth; in the Apocalypse, those whose portion and hope are in this world only. Rev. 12.
5. Inhabitant of a land, in the law of the jubile; every man to whom liberty was proclaimed in the fiftieth year. Levit. 25.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:22
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
Isaiah 24:5
The earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant.
Psalm 33:8
Let all the earth fear the LORD: let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him.
Revelation 12:12

Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.
corruption_summary: Isa 24:5 is the verse most needed and least used in modern discussion of the earth's condition, because it locates the defilement in the moral breach of a covenant by the inhabitants rather than merely in their mismanagement of resources.
corruption_paragraphs: Two frameworks now compete for the subject, and Scripture belongs to neither. One treats the earth as raw material with no claim on its inhabitants beyond usefulness, which cannot be squared with a creation God pronounced good, a land given sabbaths of its own, and a law that forbids taking the mother bird with the young. The other treats the earth as itself sacred and man as essentially a contaminant, which cannot be squared with Gen 1:28 or with the fact that man alone bears the image of God. Isa 24 gives the third account and the truer one: the earth is defiled under its inhabitants because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, and broken the everlasting covenant. The disorder in the ground is downstream of the disorder in the man, exactly as Gen 3 said — cursed is the ground for thy sake.

The pastoral use of the doctrine is in the contrast Revelation draws. The dwellers on the earth are not simply people who happen to live here; the phrase marks those whose settled portion is here and who have no other. Believers are called strangers and pilgrims, whose citizenship is in heaven, and who therefore hold their tenancy loosely without holding it carelessly. That is why the Christian can be the best possible steward of a place he does not ultimately belong to: he tends it as a trust rather than clutching it as a possession, he expects no paradise from it, and he is not driven to despair when it fails him.
roots_summary: Hebrew yōshēb is the participle of yāshab, to sit or dwell — an inhabitant is one sitting in a place. Greek katoikeō is to settle down and dwell, distinguished from paroikeō, to sojourn as a stranger.
roots_lines: Hebrew yōshēb (H3427, participle) — one dwelling, an inhabitant; from yāshab, to sit, remain, dwell.
Hebrew tēbēl (H8398) — the habitable world; the term in Psa 33:8, all the inhabitants of the world, viewing the earth as inhabited rather than as mere ground.
Greek katoikeō (G2730) — to dwell, settle, inhabit; used of them that dwell on the earth throughout Revelation.
Greek paroikeō (G3939) — to sojourn, dwell as a stranger; the contrasting word, from which parish derives, used of Abraham sojourning in the land of promise.
Greek oikoumenē (G3625) — the inhabited world; rendered the world in the decree of Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed (Luk 2:1).
usage: Of the creature's smallness before God: the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers (Isa 40:22).
Of accountability and defilement: the earth is defiled under the inhabitants thereof (Isa 24:5); let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him (Psa 33:8).
Of those whose portion is here: woe to the inhabiters of the earth (Rev 12:12), set against the saints who are strangers and pilgrims (Heb 11:13).

etymology: From Greek eidōlon, an image, phantom, or appearance, from eidos, form — the root idea is a look, a mere appearance. That is already a judgment: an idol is a seeming. The Hebrew words are blunter still. 'elīl is a diminutive playing on 'ēl, God — a godlet, a nothing; pesel is a carved thing; and gillūl, Ezekiel's favourite term, is related to a word for dung.
biblical_def: An idol is anything given the worship due to God alone, and Scripture attacks it on two fronts at once. First, idols are nothing: “we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one” (1Co 8:4). They have no being, no power, and no claim. “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4), and the psalm proceeds with devastating simplicity — mouths that speak not, eyes that see not, ears that hear not — concluding that they that make them are like unto them, which is the deepest thing Scripture says about idolatry: the worshipper is conformed to what he worships. Habakkuk presses the absurdity of the manufacture: “What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it…that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols?” (Hab 2:18). Second, and without contradiction, the worship of idols is real traffic with demons — the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God. So the idol is nothing and the idolatry is deadly. The second commandment therefore forbids not merely other gods but images of the true God: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). And the New Testament shews the gospel's effect in one clause — ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God — conversion described as a change of masters.
webster_summary: An image or anything else given the worship due to God alone; in Scripture nothing in itself, the work of men's hands, yet the occasion of real traffic with devils, forbidden by the second commandment even as a likeness of the true God, and abandoned at conversion.
webster_full: IDOL, n. 1. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship; a pagan deity.
2. An image or representation of any kind, used in worship; and hence, in Scripture, forbidden even when intended as a representation of the true God. Exod. 20.
3. A person or thing loved and honored to adoration; that on which the heart is set. Covetousness, which is idolatry. Col. 3.
4. Anything on which we set our affections; that to which we indulge an excessive and sinful attachment.
5. The Greek eidolon is a form or appearance merely; the Hebrew elil signifies a thing of nought, and gillulim a term of contempt. The names themselves pronounce the judgment.
scriptures: Exodus 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Psalm 115:4
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
1 Corinthians 8:4
As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.
1 Thessalonians 1:9
For they themselves shew of us what manner of entering in we had unto you, and how ye turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God;
corruption_summary: Idolatry is treated as an extinct problem of carved images, so that the second commandment is thought to have no modern application — while Scripture names covetousness as idolatry and the making of images of God remains as forbidden as it ever was.
corruption_paragraphs: The second commandment forbids two distinct things, and the second is regularly forgotten. It forbids other gods, and it forbids images — including images of the true God. Israel's golden calf was not offered to a rival deity; Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD, and the sin was worshipping the true God by a likeness of His own devising. Deuteronomy gives the reason explicitly: ye saw no manner of similitude on the day the LORD spake unto you in Horeb. This is why the Reformed churches removed images and why the regulative principle of worship follows from the commandment rather than being an addition to it. The question in worship is never what seems helpful but what God has commanded, and He has not commanded that He be represented.

The other half of the neglect is the assumption that idolatry ended with paganism. Paul twice defines covetousness as idolatry, and Job disclaims making gold his hope. An idol is whatever the heart trusts, fears, and serves in God's place, and it need not be carved to be worshipped — money, reputation, security, family, and the self all take the office readily. The Psalm's conclusion is the warning that gives the doctrine its bite: they that make them are like unto them. Men become like what they worship, growing as deaf and blind as their idols; and by the same law, beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, we are changed into the same image, from glory to glory. The remedy is not merely to demolish the idol but to turn, as the Thessalonians did, to the living and true God.
roots_summary: Hebrew names idols with contempt: 'elīl, a godlet or nothing; pesel, a carved image; gillūl, a term Ezekiel uses connected with dung; massēkâh, a molten image. Greek eidōlon is a mere appearance, and eidōlolatria is idol-service.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'elīl (H457) — a thing of nought, a godlet; a contemptuous diminutive echoing 'ēl, God. Used in Psa 96:5, all the gods of the nations are idols.
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven image, something hewn; the word in the second commandment (Exo 20:4).
Hebrew gillūl (H1544) — idols; Ezekiel's characteristic term, some 39 times in that book, connected with a root for dung-pellets.
Greek eidōlon (G1497) — an image, a phantom, an idol; from eidos, form or appearance — the name itself denies the thing substance.
Greek eidōlolatria (G1495) — idolatry, idol-service; listed among the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20) and identified with covetousness (Col 3:5).
usage: Of the prohibition: thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image (Exo 20:4); ye saw no manner of similitude (Deu 4:15).
Of the emptiness of idols: their idols are silver and gold (Psa 115:4); an idol is nothing in the world (1Co 8:4); what profiteth the graven image? (Hab 2:18).
Of the heart's idols and of conversion: covetousness, which is idolatry (Col 3:5); ye turned to God from idols (1Th 1:9); little children, keep yourselves from idols (1Jo 5:21).

pos: n. and v. (rendering Hebrew kābōd, kābad, and Greek timē, doxa)
etymology: From Old French onor, from Latin honor, esteem or public office; the Authorized Version's spelling with -our is retained here as the dictionary's standard. The Hebrew kābad means literally to be heavy, and its noun kābōd is weight — so that to honour someone is to treat him as weighty, and glory is heaviness. The Greek timē comes from the vocabulary of price and valuation: to honour is to reckon at a high value.
biblical_def: Honour in Scripture is the giving of due weight, and the direction of it is what makes it either obedience or idolatry. It is owed first to God: “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Pro 3:9) — honour rendered not in sentiment but in the first and best of what one has, which is why the firstfruits and not the leftovers are named. It is owed to the Son equally with the Father, and the Lord makes this a test: “That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him” (Joh 5:23) — which forecloses every religion that professes to revere God while denying Christ. It is owed to parents by the fifth commandment, the first with promise: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land” (Exo 20:12), and the Lord rebuked the Corban tradition that let a man evade the support of his parents under a show of piety. It is owed within the church to those who labour in it: “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17), where the following verse about the ox and the labourer's hire shews that material support is included. And it is owed broadly — honour all men; honour the king; in honour preferring one another.
webster_summary: The giving of due weight and value; owed to God in the firstfruits of one's substance, to the Son equally with the Father, to parents under the fifth commandment, to faithful elders in double measure, and in its measure to all men and to lawful authority.
webster_full: HONOUR, n. 1. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation; respect; veneration.
2. That which is due or paid in token of esteem; reverence; dignity; as, honour thy father and thy mother.
3. Reputation; good name; a nice sense of what is right, and of what is due to others.
4. The Hebrew word signifies weight; to honour is to account weighty, and glory is heaviness. The Greek word is from the vocabulary of price, to value highly.
5. HONOUR, v.t. To revere; to respect; to treat with deference and submission, and perform relative duties to. Honour the LORD with thy substance. Prov. 3.
scriptures: Exodus 20:12
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
Proverbs 3:9
Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
John 5:23
That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
1 Timothy 5:17
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Honour has been redefined as a feeling owed only where it is felt to be deserved, so that the commanded honour of parents, elders, and magistrates is made conditional on their merit — and, in the other direction, honour is claimed by office-holders as immunity from correction.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture attaches honour to relation and office, not to performance. The fifth commandment carries no clause exempting children of poor parents, and Peter told slaves to be subject not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward. This does not make honour unlimited: the same Scripture requires that we obey God rather than men, forbids following a father into idolatry, and provides for the rebuke and even the removal of an elder. But the modern instinct — that respect must be earned before it is given, and withdrawn the moment it is disappointed — is not the biblical one. Honour is first a duty rendered to God through the station He has appointed, and only secondarily a response to the character of the person occupying it. That is why it can be commanded at all.

The corresponding abuse belongs to those in office who invoke honour to escape accountability. Paul's instruction about elders is the pattern of the balance: double honour in one verse, and in the same passage the rule that an accusation against an elder shall be received before two or three witnesses, and that those who sin are to be rebuked before all, that others also may fear. Honour and correction are not alternatives. The Lord Himself honoured His mother from the cross and yet withstood Peter to his face; He rebuked the Pharisees for using Corban to strip the fifth commandment of its cost. Honour that never costs the giver anything is flattery, and honour that never permits correction is tyranny.
roots_summary: Hebrew kābad is to be heavy, and so to honour; its noun kābōd is weight and hence glory. Greek timē is price or value, giving timaō, to value highly; doxa is glory or reputation.
roots_lines: Hebrew kābad (H3513) — to be heavy, to be honoured, to glorify; the same verb used of Pharaoh hardening (making heavy) his heart.
Hebrew kābōd (H3519) — weight, glory, honour; the word behind the glory that filled the tabernacle and the weight of glory in 2Co 4:17.
Hebrew hādar (H1921) — to honour, to adorn, to shew respect; used in Lev 19:32, thou shalt honour the face of the old man.
Greek timē (G5092) — a valuing, price, honour; used of double honour for elders (1Ti 5:17) and of the price paid for the field of blood.
Greek timaō (G5091) — to value, to honour; the verb of the fifth commandment as quoted in the Gospels and of honouring the Son (Joh 5:23).
usage: Of honour toward God: honour the LORD with thy substance (Pro 3:9); them that honour me I will honour (1Sa 2:30).
Of honour toward Christ: that all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father (Joh 5:23).
Of honour in family, church, and commonwealth: honour thy father and thy mother (Exo 20:12); double honour for elders (1Ti 5:17); honour all men, honour the king (1Pe 2:17).
